sections.overview: Across temperate Eurasia, the mostly resident Eurasian nuthatch depends on mature trees for bark rich in food and cavities for nests.
sections.identification: Adults are 12–14.5 cm long and weigh about 19–26 g. The compact body, short tail, pointed bill, blue-grey back and black eye stripe are distinctive; European birds often have buff underparts, while northern forms are paler. Males have darker chestnut flanks than females.
sections.habitat: It favours mature deciduous or mixed woodland, especially old trees with holes. Parks and orchards also suit it when such trees remain; most populations stay year-round, while juveniles disperse and some northern birds move after poor cone crops.
sections.diet: In spring and summer it gleans caterpillars, beetles, spiders and other small invertebrates from bark, crevices and buds; nestlings receive mainly insects. Seeds and nuts matter more in autumn and winter. The bird wedges hard food into a bark crack to hammer it open, and caches surplus seeds for later.
sections.behavior: Curved claws grip bark, allowing headfirst descent. Pairs hold territories year-round. The species is highly vocal, with repeated loud whistles and sharper alarm calls.
sections.reproduction: The pair nests in a tree cavity, often an old woodpecker hole. A nuthatch narrows an oversized entrance with dried mud, leaving a small opening that limits access for larger competitors. The female usually lays six to eight eggs and incubates them for about 16–17 days. Young fledge at about 24 days and remain dependent for roughly one to two weeks.
sections.ecology: By using old woodpecker holes, the nuthatch depends on cavity-building birds as well as ageing trees. Larger competitors, such as starlings, are excluded by the mud-narrowed entrance.
sections.conservation: The species is widespread; the IUCN assessment published in 2018 classified it as Least Concern, with a stable global population. Loss and fragmentation of old woodland can still remove nest cavities and feeding surfaces, causing local declines. In Britain, monitoring records a strong increase from 1967 to 2024.
